title: Order & Ranking
summary: Rank-conversion and ordering puzzles: ranks from either end, totals from two ranks, people between two positions, queue shifts, and taller/heavier comparison chains. Two formulas (n + 1 − p and a + b − 1) plus the between-count run the entire numeric half; the comparison half is inequality chaining into one unique order. Speed comes from drawing a mini-row and from the built-in check a + b = n + 1.

subtopics.title: How ranking questions work
subtopics.concept: In a row or a queue, a person's rank tells how many people stand before them, plus one. Every ranking question comes from this one sentence. Learn two shortcuts: the rank from the other end, and the total from two ranks. Draw a small row of boxes whenever three or more people are involved.

tricks.body: For one person, the two ranks from opposite ends always add up to the total plus 1. If they do not, you have misread a number.

tricks.body: Draw a short row of boxes. 'a-th from the left' means $a - 1$ people stand before the person. Counting people at each end is often faster than any formula.

steps: People below her: $45 - 12 = 33$.
Her rank from the bottom: $33 + 1 = 34$.

mistakes.right: Underline the facing word. South-facing left is your right.

subtopics.notes:
### The one idea
A rank counts the person too. If 4 people stand before you, your rank is 5.

> **Rule:** Rank = number of people before you + 1. Every formula in this topic comes from this line.

Example: Sita is 5th in a queue of 12. Four people are ahead of her ($5 - 1 = 4$). Seven are behind her ($12 - 5 = 7$).

### The other end
The same person has a different rank from the other end. Find it in one step.

$$\text{rank from the other end} = \text{total} - \text{rank} + 1$$

Example: in a row of 40, Ravi is 10th from the left. From the right he is $40 - 10 + 1 = 31$st.

Why add 1? Ravi is counted once from each side. Take him out and count the people to his right: $40 - 10 = 30$. Then add Ravi himself.

### Total from two ranks
Suppose one person is $a$-th from one end and $b$-th from the other end. Both counts include that person. So he is counted twice.

$$\text{total} = a + b - 1$$

Example: 9th from the left and 11th from the right gives $9 + 11 - 1 = 19$ people.

> **Tip:** The two ranks always add up to the total plus 1. Use this to check yourself: $9 + 11 = 20 = 19 + 1$.

### Ahead and behind
"Ahead" does not include the person. So it is one less than his rank.

- Ahead of him = rank $- 1$.
- Behind him = total $-$ rank.
- Ahead + behind + 1 = total.

Example: 14 people are ahead of a girl and 21 are behind her. The total is $14 + 21 + 1 = 36$.

### Two people swap places
When two people exchange seats, each person takes the other's seat. So a new rank is just the old rank of the other seat.

Example: a row has 25 people. Ram is 8th from the left. Shyam is 9th from the right, which is $25 + 1 - 9 = 17$th from the left. After the swap, Ram is 17th from the left.

> **Watch:** Convert both ranks to the same end before you compare seats.

### Stacks and rows of objects
Books, boxes and shelves work the same way. "Above" is like "to the left". Write the order from top to bottom as each sentence comes. Then read the seat that is asked.

### A full walk-through
Read this one slowly. A queue has 52 people. Kavya is 17th from the front.

1. People ahead of her: $17 - 1 = 16$.
2. People behind her: $52 - 17 = 35$.
3. Check: $16 + 35 + 1 = 52$. The total matches.
4. Her rank from the back: $35 + 1 = 36$. The formula gives the same: $52 + 1 - 17 = 36$.

> **Example:** Two ways gave 36. When both routes agree, you can trust the answer. Use this check in the exam whenever time allows.

### Facing South
A row facing North has its usual left and right. A row facing **South** has them swapped. Their left is your right. Underline the facing word before you use any left or right clue.

patterns.name: Building a stack or row from clues

steps: Draw a column or a row of empty boxes.
Fill in the sure fact first, such as 'at the bottom'.

steps: T is at the bottom.
Order from the top: P, Q, R, S, T.
The middle (third) box is R.

patterns.name: People ahead and behind

Add the person himself: +1.

patterns.name: Exactly in the middle
patterns.howToSpot: The person is exactly in the middle, or there are as many people ahead as behind.
steps: Write ahead = behind, so $r - 1 = n - r$.
Solve for the total: $n = 2r - 1$.
The middle person is in seat $\dfrac{n+1}{2}$.
patterns.why: The middle person has the same number of people on each side.

steps: Ahead of her: $13 - 1 = 12$.
Behind her: also 12.

subtopics.title: Ranks and positions
subtopics.concept: These questions are about one person's rank in a class, a queue or a row. Use the two shortcuts: total minus rank plus 1, and rank plus rank minus 1. When people join or leave the row, count the people before him first. Then add 1.

subtopics.notes:
### The other end, again
The rank from the other end of a class or a row is a simple sum.

$$\text{rank from the bottom} = \text{class size} - \text{rank from the top} + 1$$

Example: in a class of 60, Neha is 23rd from the top. From the bottom she is $60 - 23 + 1 = 38$th.

### The total from two ranks
If a person's two ranks are given, the total is their sum minus 1.

Example: Sonu is 14th from the left and 20th from the right. The row has $14 + 20 - 1 = 33$ people.

Three quick facts to remember:
- 12th from the top in a class of 45 is 34th from the bottom.
- 8th from the left and 21st from the right gives $8 + 21 - 1 = 28$ people.
- 11th from either end gives $11 + 11 - 1 = 21$ people.

> **Tip:** The total is always bigger than each of the two ranks. If not, you misread.

### People above and below
The rank counts the person too. The number of people below him leaves him out.

- People below him = class size $-$ his rank from the top.
- People above him = his rank from the top $- 1$.

Example: Reena is 12th from the top in a class of 40. So $40 - 12 = 28$ students are below her.

### People join or leave the front
Count the people before him first. Then add 1.

- $k$ people join **ahead** of him: his rank becomes old rank $+ k$.
- $k$ people who were **ahead** of him leave: his rank becomes old rank $- k$.
- People who join or leave **behind** him do not change his rank from the front.

Example: Ishaan is 18th in a queue. 6 people join in front of him. Then 3 people who were ahead of him leave. His new rank is $18 + 6 - 3 = 21$st.

### People leave from the middle of a row
Only the people to the right of the leavers move. They slide left by the number who left.

Example: A is 16th from the left. 5 people leave from the left end. A slides to $16 - 5 = 11$th.

> **Watch:** Look at where the leavers stood. People on the same side as the person change his rank. People on the other side change only the total.

### Rank from the other end after people leave
When people to his left leave, his rank from the right does not change. Only the total falls.

Example: in a row of 45, Gopal is 20th from the left. His rank from the right is $45 + 1 - 20 = 26$. Eight people to his left leave. He is now 12th from the left in a row of 37. His rank from the right is $37 + 1 - 12 = 26$. It did not change.

### Class ranks with a twist
If some students fail, remove them from the total before you use the formula. The formula stays the same. Only the total changes.

Example: a class of 50 has 4 failed students, and Anil is 10th from the top among the rest. Now the total is $50 - 4 = 46$. His rank from the bottom is $46 + 1 - 10 = 37$.

patterns.howToSpot: People join or leave a queue. The person's new position is asked.
steps: Count only the people who joined or left ahead of him.
Add joiners and subtract leavers from his rank.

steps: After the joiners: $18 + 6 = 24$.

patterns.howToSpot: Some people stand up and leave. A remaining person's new rank is asked.
steps: Note whether the leavers stood on his left or right.
Recount his rank from the side where they left. Subtract the leavers.

From the right: $37 + 1 - 12 = 26$.

subtopics.title: People between two positions
subtopics.concept: These questions ask how many people stand between two people. First find out which end each rank comes from. If both ranks are from the same end, subtract and take away 1. If they are from opposite ends, subtract both from the total.

formulas.name: Between, same end
formulas.note: Both ranks are counted from the same end.

formulas.name: Between, opposite ends
formulas.note: n = total people, a and b = ranks from opposite ends.

formulas.name: Middle person
formulas.note: a and b from the same end. The result must be a whole number.

formulas.name: Rank from the gap
formulas.note: k people are between a and b, counted from the same end.

tricks.title: Convert first, then count
tricks.body: Never subtract ranks from different ends. Convert one rank with $n + 1 - p$. Then use the same-end formula.

example.q: In a row of 40, A is 5th from the left and B is 10th from the right. How many people are between them?
steps: B from the left: $40 + 1 - 10 = 31$.

mistakes.wrong: Subtracting a rank from the left from a rank from the right.
mistakes.right: Convert one rank to the other end first, or use $n - a - b$.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the last -1 and counting the two people as well.
mistakes.right: 'Between' leaves out both people.

mistakes.wrong: Converting both ranks with $n + 1 - p$.
mistakes.right: Convert only one. Both ranks must end up on the same side.

mistakes.wrong: Using the person's old seat after a swap.
mistakes.right: After a swap, the person sits in the other's seat.

mistakes.wrong: Continuing when the answer is negative.
mistakes.right: A negative count means a misread end. Stop and convert again.

subtopics.notes:
### The same end
"Between" leaves out both people. So subtract the two ranks and drop 1.

$$\text{between} = |a - b| - 1$$

Example: R is 9th from the top and S is 26th from the top. Between them: $26 - 9 - 1 = 16$ students.

### Opposite ends
Suppose P is $a$-th from the left and Q is $b$-th from the right. Take both ranks off the total. What is left is the people in between.

$$\text{between} = \text{total} - a - b$$

Example: a row has 45 people. X is 14th from the left and Y is 18th from the right. Between them: $45 - 14 - 18 = 13$.

> **Tip:** No total given? Find it from any person who has ranks from both ends: $a + b - 1$.

### The middle person
Take two ranks from the same end. The person exactly in the middle has this rank from that end:

$$\dfrac{a + b}{2}$$

Example: 9th and 21st from the left. The middle person is $\dfrac{9 + 21}{2} = 15$th from the left. There are 5 people on each side of him, between him and each of the two.

If $a + b$ is odd, there is no single middle person. Two people stand in the middle.

### The overlap puzzle
A swap can reveal a rank that the row never stated. Build the total first. Then count between.

Example: Ravi is 15th from the left. Sohan is 11th from the right. After they swap, Ravi is 20th from the left.

1. Ravi took Sohan's seat. So Sohan's seat is 20th from the left and 11th from the right.
2. Total $= 20 + 11 - 1 = 30$.
3. Originally, Ravi was 15th and Sohan's seat was 20th. Between them: $20 - 15 - 1 = 4$.

> **Watch:** The rank after the swap belongs to the other person's seat. It is not his old seat.

### Given the gap, find the rank
If $k$ people stand between two people and they are counted from the same end, the second rank is:

$$b = a + k + 1$$

Example: Tina is 11th from the top. 7 students are between Tina and Uma, and Uma is below her. Uma is $11 + 7 + 1 = 19$th from the top.

### People outside the pair
"How many people are not between them?" Find between first. Then remove the two people themselves.

$$\text{outside} = \text{total} - \text{between} - 2$$

Example: total 52, between 16. Outside: $52 - 16 - 2 = 34$.

### Two ways to check
Check every answer once by drawing the row.

Example: the row has 45 people. X is 14th from the left. Y is 18th from the right, so Y is $45 + 1 - 18 = 28$th from the left. Now use the same-end formula: $28 - 14 - 1 = 13$. The direct formula $45 - 14 - 18 = 13$ agrees.

Two routes, one answer. If they differ, one rank was read from the wrong end.

> **Note:** Between can never be negative, and between plus 2 can never be more than the total. If it is, you misread an end.

Add them and halve the sum.

patterns.name: Swap and count between
patterns.howToSpot: A swap gives a new rank. The number of people between the two before the swap is asked.
steps: The person who moved took the other's seat. That seat has the new rank.
Find the total: new rank $+$ other's rank from the other end $- 1$.

steps: Sohan's seat is 20th from the left and 11th from the right. Total $= 20 + 11 - 1 = 30$.

patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how many people are not between two people, or ahead of and behind them.
steps: Find the people between first.
Subtract that from the total.
Subtract 2 for the two people themselves.
patterns.why: Total = between + the two people + everyone outside.

Add the gap $k$ and 1 to the nearer rank.
Subtract instead if the second person is closer to the start.
patterns.why: The second person sits after the $k$ people between and one more seat.

subtopics.title: Ordering and comparison chains
subtopics.concept: These questions give scattered comparisons such as 'A is taller than B'. Write each clue as a short arrow. Join the arrows into one chain, then read the seat that is asked. Words like 'shorter', 'younger' and 'below' point the arrow the other way, so turn them around first.

tricks.title: Write two symbols for each clue
tricks.body: Turn each sentence into two letters with a sign, such as S < V. Keep the sign pointing the same way all through. The reversed words then become easy to see.

example.q: Sunil is younger than Vijay. Vijay is younger than Wasim. Who is the oldest?
steps: Arrows: Vijay > Sunil, Wasim > Vijay.
Chain: Wasim > Vijay > Sunil.

tricks.title: Start from the person named most often
tricks.body: The person who appears in the most clues is the best starting point. Build the chain outwards from that person and it forms in one pass.

example.q: A is taller than B. B is taller than D. C is taller than A. Who is the tallest?
steps: B appears twice. Chain B > D.
A is above B: A > B > D.
C is above A: C > A > B > D.

mistakes.wrong: Answering from part of the chain before using every clue.
mistakes.right: Use all the clues, then read the chain.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'younger than' or 'less than' in the surface direction.
mistakes.right: Turn every clue so the bigger, older or higher person is on the left.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring the word 'immediately'.
mistakes.right: It means directly next to. It can change who is second or third.

mistakes.wrong: Accepting two possible orders.
mistakes.right: A full puzzle has exactly one order. Read the clues again.

mistakes.wrong: Building the whole order when the seat is already fixed.
mistakes.right: Check whether only one person can fill the seat asked.

subtopics.notes:
### Write each clue as an arrow
Use one arrow for one clue. Point it towards the taller, older or higher person.

- "A is taller than B" becomes A > B.
- "C is shorter than B" becomes B > C.
- "D scored less than C" becomes C > D.

> **Rule:** Always put the bigger, older or higher person on the left. Turn 'shorter', 'younger', 'less' and 'below' around before you write.

### Join the arrows into a chain
Clues that share a person join together. A > B and B > D make A > B > D.

Example: "A is taller than B. C is taller than D and shorter than B. E is shorter than D." Write A > B, B > C > D and D > E. The chain is A > B > C > D > E. The second tallest is B.

### Read the seat
Read the chain from the left end.

- Tallest: the first person.
- Shortest: the last person.
- Second tallest: the second person from the left.

The middle seat of five people is the third one.

### When the full order is not known
Some clues leave two people unranked. For example, A > B and C > D say nothing about A against C. So the whole order is open.

But the answer may still be fixed. If only one person can stand first, that person is the tallest, even when other seats stay open.

> **Tip:** Fix the seat that is asked. You do not always need the full order.

### Marks, ages and objects
Marks, ages, heights and weights all work alike. Use the same arrows for all of them.

Objects in a stack work alike too. "The red box is above the blue box" is an arrow pointing up. Write the stack from the top down and read it like a chain. "Third from the top" is the third person in the chain.

### Words that fix a place
Some words fix a place more tightly than a simple "taller than".

- "Immediately above B" means directly next to B, with no one between.
- "Between B and D" means somewhere in the middle. It does not say the exact seat.

Use "immediately" clues first. They join two people into one block.

> **Watch:** Read the clue again if you find two possible orders. A full puzzle has one order only.

### A slow example
Read the clues once, then write the arrows. "Ann is older than Ben. Cara is younger than Ben. Dev is older than Ann." Arrows: Ann > Ben, Ben > Cara, Dev > Ann. Chain: Dev > Ann > Ben > Cara. The youngest is Cara. The second oldest is Ann.

> **Example:** Ask a different question of the same chain. Who is older than Ben but younger than Dev? Only Ann fits. Reading the chain answers every version of the question.

### Facing pairs
Two people who face each other have opposite left and right. The left hand of one is the right hand of the other. Draw the two arrows first.

patterns.howToSpot: Clues use 'taller than', 'bigger than' or 'heavier than'. The tallest, shortest or one seat is asked.
steps: Write each clue as an arrow with the taller person first.
Join clues that share a person.
Read the chain from the left.
patterns.why: Clues that share a person always join into a single line.

example.q: A is taller than B. C is taller than D and shorter than B. E is shorter than D. Who is the second tallest?
steps: Arrows: A > B, B > C > D, D > E.
Chain: A > B > C > D > E.
The second person from the left is B.

patterns.name: Marks and scores
patterns.howToSpot: Clues use 'scored more than' or 'scored less than'. The highest, lowest or an exact seat is asked.
steps: Write each clue as an arrow towards the higher score.
Turn 'less than' around.
Join the arrows and read the chain.
patterns.why: 'Scored more' works exactly like 'taller'.

example.q: Kiran scored more than Lata but less than Manu. Neeta scored less than Lata. Om scored more than Manu. Who scored the second highest?
steps: Arrows: Manu > Kiran > Lata, Lata > Neeta, Om > Manu.
Chain: Om > Manu > Kiran > Lata > Neeta.
The second person from the left is Manu.

patterns.name: Ages with 'younger' and 'older'
patterns.howToSpot: Clues use 'older than' and 'younger than' about three to six people.
steps: Put the older person on the left in every arrow.
Turn each 'younger than' clue around.
Join and count from the left.
patterns.why: Turning every clue to the same direction stops sign slips.

example.q: Rita is younger than Sita. Tina is older than Sita. Uma is younger than Rita. Vani is older than Tina. Who is the third oldest?
steps: Arrows: Sita > Rita, Tina > Sita, Rita > Uma, Vani > Tina.
Chain: Vani > Tina > Sita > Rita > Uma.
The third person from the left is Sita.

patterns.name: Stacked books and boxes
patterns.howToSpot: Books, boxes or subjects are described as above or below. A seat from the top or the bottom is asked.
steps: Turn each 'below' clue into an 'above' clue.
Write the stack from the top down as a chain.
Count from the asked end.
patterns.why: 'Above' is just the arrow pointing up.

example.q: Five books are in a stack. Maths is above Science. History is below Science. Art is above Maths but below English. Which book is in the middle?
steps: Arrows: Maths above Science, Science above History, English above Art above Maths.
Stack from the top: English, Art, Maths, Science, History.
The middle (third) book is Maths.

patterns.name: The seat is fixed but the order is not
patterns.howToSpot: Some pairs are never compared, but the question asks only for the tallest, shortest or one seat.
steps: Draw the arrows you have.
Check who has nobody above them. If only one person, that is the first seat.
Ignore the pairs that are never compared.
patterns.why: A seat can be fixed even when the whole order is open.

example.q: P is taller than Q. Q is taller than R. S is taller than P. T is shorter than S. Who is the tallest?
steps: Arrows: S > P > Q > R and S > T.
T is below S, but T is not compared with P, Q or R.
Nobody is above S.

patterns.name: Clues with 'immediately' and 'between'
patterns.howToSpot: Clues say 'immediately above' or 'between'. An exact rank is asked.
steps: Join 'immediately' pairs into one block first.
Place the other people above or below the block.
Fit each 'between' clue into the gap.
patterns.why: An 'immediately' pair is a fixed block, and the other clues only place things around it.

example.q: Five students are ranked by marks. A is ranked immediately above B. C is ranked above A. D is ranked below B. E is ranked between B and D. Who is ranked 4th?
steps: A and B form a block: A, B. C is above the block.
D is below B, and E is between B and D.
Order: C, A, B, E, D. Rank 4 is E.

revision: Every clue is an arrow towards the bigger, older or higher person.
Join clues that share a person into one chain.
Turn 'shorter', 'younger', 'less' and 'below' around first.
Read the chain: tallest is the first, shortest is the last.
A seat can be fixed even if the whole order is open.
'Immediately' means next to. 'Between' means somewhere inside.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Rank conversion at the two ends
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A rank from one end plus a total; the other end is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Mirror: total − rank + 1; queues: ahead = rank − 1, behind = total − rank.

example.q: **In a queue of 60, S is 21st from the front. How many people are behind her?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One person's rank from both ends; class size asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Add the ranks and subtract 1; the shared person was counted twice.

example.q: **A is 9th from the left and 11th from the right. How many people are in the row?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many between A and B' with ranks from the same or opposite ends.
pyqPatterns.approach: Same end: |a − b| − 1. Opposite ends with total T: T − a − b. Convert ends before subtracting.

example.q: **P is 11th from the left and Q is 9th from the right in a row of 30. How many sit between?**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who is exactly in the middle of A and B?'
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert to the same end; the midpoint is (a + b) / 2 from that end.

example.q: **Manish is 14th from the left; Rakesh is 8th from the right in a row of 35. Who is midway between them?**
example.solution: Rakesh = $35 - 8 + 1 = 28$th from the left; midway = $(14 + 28)/2$ = **21st from the left**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Comparison chain to a named slot
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Taller/older/more-marks clues; tallest, youngest or Nth is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Arrows toward the bigger/older/better; merge into a chain; read the slot; reversed words flip the arrow.

example.q: **M > N; O < N; P > M; Q < O. Who is second highest?**
example.solution: P > M > N > O > Q → second highest = **M**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Above/below clues for boxes, books or shelves; a slot is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Above = arrow up; stack the chain on paper; read 'Nth from top' directly off the list.

example.q: **Red above Blue; Green below Blue but above White; Yellow at the bottom. Which is second from the top?**
example.solution: Red, Blue, Green, White, Yellow → second = **Blue**.

solvedExamples.q: In a class of **40 students**, Meena ranks **15th from the top**. What is her rank from the bottom?
solvedExamples.solution: Rank from the other end = 40 + 1 − 15 = **26th**. (25th forgets the +1.)

solvedExamples.q: In a row of students, **Karan is 12th from the left and 19th from the right.** How many students are in the row?
solvedExamples.solution: n = 12 + 19 − 1 = **30**. Check: 11 students left of him + Karan + 18 to his right = 30 ✓.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add the two ranks, subtract one.

solvedExamples.q: **A is taller than B. C is taller than A. D is taller than C but shorter than E.** Who is the **third tallest**?
solvedExamples.solution: Chain the statements: E > D > C > A > B. Third tallest = **C**. (The chain is forced — each statement slots exactly one person.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Build one chain E > D > C > A > B and read the slot; no trial and error needed.

solvedExamples.q: In a row of **36 students, A is 15th from the left and B is 9th from the right.** How many students sit **between** A and B?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Convert the right-rank to a left-rank first; then difference minus one.

practice.q: In a class of **45 students, Ravi ranks 12th from the top**. What is his rank from the bottom?
In a row of students, **Sita is 8th from the left and 21st from the right.** How many students are in the row?
practice.shortcut: Sum of the two ranks minus 1.

practice.q: In a row of **40 students, A is 11th from the left end.** What is A's position from the right end?
practice.shortcut: Mirror formula n + 1 − p.

practice.q: In a row of **30 students, A is 10th from the left and B is 12th from the right.** How many students are **between** A and B?
practice.solution: B from the left = 30 + 1 − 12 = 19th. Between = 19 − 10 − 1 = **8**.
practice.shortcut: Convert B to a left-rank, subtract, drop the endpoints.

practice.q: In a queue of **50 people, X is 16th from the front and Y is 20th from the back.** How many people are **between** X and Y?
practice.solution: Y from the front = 50 + 1 − 20 = 31st. Between = 31 − 16 − 1 = **14**.
practice.shortcut: Same-end conversion first; then difference − 1.

practice.q: In a queue, **A is 9th from the front and B is 21st from the front.** Who stands **exactly in the middle** of A and B (in position, not count)?
practice.solution: Middle position = (9 + 21) ÷ 2 = **15th from the front**. (The count of people between them is 11 — different question.)
practice.shortcut: Average the two same-end positions.

practice.q: **Bulbul is 11th from either end of a queue.** How many people are in the queue?
practice.solution: n = 11 + 11 − 1 = **21**. (She is the exact middle of an odd-length queue.)
practice.shortcut: 'Either end' means both ranks are the same number.

practice.q: **A is 17th from the left and 18th from the right in a row.** How many people are in the row?
**P is taller than Q but shorter than R. S is the tallest of all. T is shorter than Q.** Who is the **second tallest**?
practice.solution: Chain: S > R > P > Q > T. Second tallest = **R**. (S is fixed at the top by 'tallest of all'; R > P > Q comes from the other statements.)
practice.shortcut: Pin the extreme first ('tallest of all'), then chain the rest.

practice.q: **A is heavier than B. C is lighter than B. D is heavier than A. E is lighter than C.** Who is the **lightest**?
practice.solution: Chain: D > A > B > C > E. Lightest = **E**. (Each 'lighter than' points downward; the chain bottoms out at E.)
practice.shortcut: One chain from the heaviest statement to the lightest; the last name is the answer.

practice.q: In a test, **M scored more than N, O scored less than N, P scored more than M, and Q scored less than M but more than N.** Who scored the **highest**?
practice.solution: Chain: P > M > Q > N > O. Highest = **P**. (Q sits between M and N, exactly as stated.)
practice.shortcut: 'More than' chains head upward; the chain's top is the answer.

practice.q: In a class test, **Mohan ranks 13th from the top and 57th from the bottom.** How many students appeared for the test?
practice.shortcut: a + b − 1, then sanity-check a + b = n + 1.

practice.q: In a queue of 30 people, **A is 9th from the front. If 5 new people join the queue at the front**, what is A's new position from the front?
practice.solution: Every old position shifts back by 5: 9 + 5 = **14th**. (The queue length also grows to 35, but only front-joins affect A's rank.)
practice.shortcut: Front joiners push the tracked person back one-for-one.

practice.q: In a row of **40 students, A is 15th from the left and B is 25th from the left.** If **A and B interchange their positions**, what is **B's new position from the right**?
practice.solution: After the swap B occupies A's old spot: 15th from the left. From the right = 40 + 1 − 15 = **26th**.
practice.shortcut: An interchange just re-labels the two positions — reuse the mirror formula on the new spot.

practice.q: **X is older than Y. Z is younger than W. V is older than X. W is older than V. Y is older than Z.** Who is the **third oldest**?
practice.solution: Chain: W > V > X > Y > Z (W is pinned above V; V above X; X above Y; Y above Z; and Z < W is automatic). Third oldest = **X**.
practice.shortcut: Build the spine W > V > X, then hang Y and Z below X.

practice.q: **In a row of 40 students, Ravi is 10th from the left end. What is his position from the right end?**
practice.solution: Mirror: $40 - 10 + 1$ = **31st** from the right (the +1 counts Ravi himself once).
practice.shortcut: Other end = total − rank + 1.

practice.q: **Meena is 17th from the right end in a queue of 30 people. What is her position from the left end?**
practice.solution: Mirror: $30 - 17 + 1$ = **14th** from the left.
practice.shortcut: The formula works in both directions.

practice.q: **A person is 9th from the left end and 11th from the right end of a row. How many people are in the row?**
practice.solution: Two ranks of the same person: total = $9 + 11 - 1$ = **19** (the −1 removes the double count).

practice.q: **In a row, a student is 23rd from the left and 12th from the right. How many students are in the row?**
practice.solution: Total = $23 + 12 - 1$ = **34** students.
practice.shortcut: Add the ranks, drop one.

practice.q: **In a row of 25 students, Ram is 8th from the left and Shyam is 9th from the right. They interchange places. What is Ram's new position from the left?**
practice.solution: Shyam's seat from the left: $25 - 9 + 1$ = 17th. Ram takes exactly that seat → **17th** from the left.
practice.shortcut: Convert the partner's rank to the asked end; that is the new seat.

practice.q: **In a row of 20 students, Ajay is 7th from the left and Vijay is 12th from the right. If they swap places, what is Vijay's new position from the left?**
practice.solution: Vijay takes Ajay's seat → **7th** from the left. (Ajay moves to Vijay's old seat, 9th from the left.)
practice.shortcut: After a swap each person simply sits where the partner sat.

practice.q: **Five boxes are stacked: Red is above Blue; Green is below Blue but above White; Yellow is at the bottom. Which box is at the top?**
practice.solution: Build top to bottom: Red > Blue > Green > White > Yellow → top = **Red**.
practice.shortcut: 'Above' is an arrow pointing up; stack as you read.

practice.q: **Six books: P is above Q; R is below Q; S is above P; U lies between P and Q; T is at the bottom. Which book is **third from the top**?**
practice.solution: S above P above Q; U between P and Q; R below Q; T last → S, P, U, Q, R, T. Third = **U**.
practice.shortcut: Chain the above/below clues, slot U into the gap, pin T at the bottom.

practice.q: **45 students stand in a row and R is exactly in the middle. What is R's position from the left end?**
practice.solution: Middle of 45: $(45 + 1)/2$ = **23rd**. Check by mirror: $45 - 23 + 1 = 23$ ✓ — the same from both ends.
practice.shortcut: Odd count: middle = (total + 1)/2 from either end.

practice.q: **In a row, A is 7th from the left end and B is 9th from the right end. A and B sit in adjacent positions with nobody between them. How many people are in the row?**
practice.solution: Adjacent → B is immediately after A: B is 8th from the left. Total = B's two ranks: $8 + 9 - 1$ = **16**. Check: A 7th, B 8th, $16 - 9 + 1 = 8$ ✓.
practice.shortcut: Adjacency fixes the second person's other-end rank; then a + b − 1.

practice.q: **Five friends sit in a row: P is to the left of Q; R is to the right of Q; S sits between P and Q; T is at the extreme right. Who sits second from the left?**
practice.solution: P left of Q with S between → P, S, Q; R to the right of Q → P, S, Q, R; T at the extreme right → P, S, Q, R, T. Second = **S**.
practice.shortcut: Chain the left-of clues; the extreme seat pins the last slot.

practice.q: **In a queue of 60 people, S is 21st from the front. How many people are behind her?**
practice.solution: Behind = total − rank = $60 - 21$ = **39** (S herself is not behind).
practice.shortcut: Behind = T − rank; ahead = rank − 1.

practice.q: **In a class of 60 students, Neha ranks 23rd from the top. What is her rank from the bottom?**
practice.solution: $60 - 23 + 1$ = **38th** from the bottom.
practice.shortcut: Bottom rank = size − top rank + 1.

practice.q: **Sonu is 14th from the left end and 20th from the right end of a row. How many people are in the row?**
practice.shortcut: Ranks add to total + 1.

practice.q: **In a queue of 35 people, Moni is 12th from the front. If 8 people ahead of her leave the queue, what is Moni's new position?**
practice.solution: 8 people ahead left → everyone behind them slides forward: $12 - 8$ = **4th** from the front.
practice.shortcut: Leavers ahead of you: rank − k. Leavers behind: no change.

practice.q: **A is 16th from the left in a row of 40 people. If 5 people leave the row from the left end, what is A's new rank from the left?**
practice.solution: The 5 departed were ahead of A (positions 1-5); A slides left by 5 → $16 - 5$ = **11th**.
practice.shortcut: Exits to your left subtract; exits to your right leave your rank alone.

practice.q: **A is 7th from the left end and B is 19th from the left end of a row. How many people are between them?**
practice.solution: Same end: $|19 - 7| - 1$ = **11** people between.
practice.shortcut: Same-end gap minus the two named people.

practice.q: **In a class, R ranks 9th from the top and S ranks 26th from the top. How many students rank between them?**
practice.solution: Same end (top): $|26 - 9| - 1$ = **16** students.
practice.shortcut: Difference of ranks minus one.

practice.q: **P is 11th from the left end and Q is 9th from the right end of a row of 30 people. How many people are between them?**
practice.solution: Opposite ends: $30 - 11 - 9$ = **10** between.
practice.shortcut: Total minus both ranks.

practice.q: **In a row of 45 students, X is 14th from the left and Y is 18th from the right. How many students are between them?**
practice.shortcut: Opposite ends: T − a − b.

practice.q: **A is 9th from the left end and B is 21st from the left end. Which position is exactly in the middle between A and B?**
practice.solution: Midpoint of the same-end ranks: $(9 + 21)/2$ = **15th from the left**.
practice.shortcut: Average of the two positions.

practice.q: **Manish is 14th from the left and Rakesh is 8th from the right in a row of 35. Which position is exactly midway between them?**
practice.solution: Rakesh from the left: $35 - 8 + 1$ = 28th. Midway: $(14 + 28)/2$ = **21st from the left**.
practice.shortcut: Mirror one rank first; then average.

practice.q: **A is 9th from the left end and 16th from the right end of a row. B is 14th from the right end. How many people sit between A and B?**
practice.solution: Row size from A: $9 + 16 - 1$ = 24. B from the left: $24 - 14 + 1$ = 11th. Between A (9th) and B (11th): $|11 - 9| - 1$ = **1** person.
practice.shortcut: Build the total from the both-ends person, convert B, then count.

practice.q: **Ram is 17th from the left and Shyam is 9th from the right in a row. After they interchange places, Ram becomes 22nd from the left. How many students sat between Ram and Shyam originally?**
practice.solution: Ram's new seat is Shyam's old one, still 9th from the right → total = $22 + 9 - 1$ = 30. Shyam's old seat from the left: $30 - 9 + 1$ = 22nd. Between originally: $22 - 17 - 1$ = **4**.
practice.shortcut: The swap pins Ram's seat to both ends → total; then a plain same-end count.

practice.q: **In a class, V ranks 18th from the top and W ranks 31st from the top. How many students lie between them?**
practice.solution: Same end: $|31 - 18| - 1$ = **12** students.
practice.shortcut: Rank difference minus one.

practice.q: **A is taller than B; C is taller than A; D is shorter than B. Who is the shortest?**
practice.solution: Chain: C > A > B > D → shortest = **D**.
practice.shortcut: Arrow toward the taller; the tail of the chain is the shortest.

practice.q: **P is taller than Q; R is shorter than S; Q is taller than S. Who is the tallest?**
practice.solution: Merge: P > Q, Q > S, S > R → P > Q > S > R → tallest = **P**.
practice.shortcut: Chain head = tallest.

practice.q: **In a test, A scored more than B; C scored less than D; B scored more than D. Who scored the least?**
practice.solution: Convert 'less' clues: C < D → D > C. Merge: A > B > D > C → least = **C**.
practice.shortcut: Flip every 'less than' sentence before chaining.

practice.q: **Five students: M scored more than N; O scored fewer than N; P scored more than M; Q scored fewer than O. Who is the second highest scorer?**
practice.solution: Convert: P > M, M > N, N > O, O > Q → P > M > N > O > Q. Second highest = **M**.
practice.shortcut: 'Fewer than' arrows flip; then read slot 2 of the chain.

practice.q: **Rahul is older than Vijay; Sunil is younger than Vijay; Anil is older than Rahul. Who is the youngest?**
practice.solution: Anil > Rahul > Vijay > Sunil → youngest = **Sunil**.
practice.shortcut: 'Younger than' points the arrow the other way; chain and read the tail.

practice.q: **A is older than B but younger than C; D is older than C. Who is the second oldest?**
practice.solution: A > B, C > A, D > C → D > C > A > B → second oldest = **C**.
practice.shortcut: 'Younger than' hides the C > A link — flip it, then merge.

practice.q: **On a shelf: Civics is below Geography; History is below Economics but above Geography; Political Science is at the bottom. Which subject is third from the top?**
practice.solution: Economics > History > Geography > Civics > Political Science → third from the top = **Geography**.
practice.shortcut: 'Below' = lower in the stack; build top-down and read slot 3.

practice.q: **Six poles: A is taller than B; B is taller than C; C is taller than E; E is taller than D; D is taller than F. Which pole is the third tallest?**
practice.solution: A > B > C > E > D > F → third tallest = **C**.
practice.shortcut: One merged chain; third from the head is the answer.

practice.q: **In a queue of 48 people, Mohan is 30th from the front. What is his position from the back?**
practice.solution: $48 - 30 + 1$ = **19th** from the back.
practice.shortcut: Back rank = queue size − front rank + 1.

practice.q: **In a class, Kishan is 18th from the top and 42nd from the bottom. How many students are in the class?**
practice.shortcut: Kishan is counted in both ranks — drop one.

practice.q: **In a queue, Tanvi is 20th from the front. If 12 people join the queue ahead of her, what is her new position from the front?**
practice.solution: 12 people now stand ahead of her who were not there before → $20 + 12$ = **32nd** from the front.
practice.shortcut: Joiners ahead: rank + k. Joiners behind: no change.

practice.q: **In a row of 30 people, B is 12th from the right end. If 4 people leave the row from the right end, what is B's new rank from the right?**
practice.solution: The 4 departed were to B's right (positions 1-4 from the right); B slides right-ward in rank: $12 - 4$ = **8th** from the right.
practice.shortcut: Exits on the side you are counting from subtract; the other side changes nothing.
